passage: Transcript, works meeting, Calderford Model Engineering Society, the track extension. Chair Bidwell: The ground survey for the raised track extension is back. Summary from the track master. Track Master Onslow: The good news: the route through the copse works, gradients under 1 in 80 the whole way, which the locomotives will thank us for. The bad news: the survey found the drainage from the car park runs exactly where pier 14 through pier 19 must stand, eighteen inches down, a live clay pipe from the 1970s that appears on no drawing anyone possesses. Bidwell: Options. Onslow: Divert the drain, 3,100 dollars by the contractor's estimate, or redesign the curve outward onto the meadow strip, which adds 40 meters of track, twelve more piers, and, by my costing, 2,800 in materials, but, and here is the argument, the wider curve lets us run the big passenger trucks on public days, which the tight curve never would. Treasurer Pike: So the cheaper option is also the better railway. Suspicious. Onslow: The drain did us a favor, I admit it freely. Pike: Funds: the extension budget holds 4,000, plus the Hollis bequest of 2,000 restricted to, his will says, making the railway more glorious, which the wider curve arguably is. Bidwell: Arguably? Pike: The executor is our own Mr. Grimes, who drives the goods train on Sundays. He has pre-approved the glory, in writing. Laughter. Bidwell: Motion: meadow curve redesign, 2,800 from general extension funds, big trucks ordered against the bequest, drain left in peace and marked on our drawings for whoever digs next, because we are not leaving the trap we fell into. Moved Onslow, seconded Pike. Carried, eleven to nil. Winter working parties Saturdays, bacon rolls at ten, the immutable clause.
question: What gradient does the route through the copse keep under?

passage: Verbatim minutes, Aldenmere Swimming Association, open water section, season safety review. Section Leader Voss: Attendance twelve, apologies three, the lake temperature this morning was 11 degrees and four of you swam anyway before this meeting, which brings me directly to item one: the buddy rule. This season logged 2,100 individual swims by the sign-in board, and the board shows 46 solo swims, every one against section rules, and I have the initials, and the initials are mostly the same initials. Mr. Krall: If the water is flat and I stay inside the buoy line, the risk is mine. Voss: The recovery is not, Mr. Krall. The rule stands because the person who pulls you out was never asked whether they accepted your risk. This is the whole argument and I am not reopening it; I am announcing enforcement: next season the board goes digital, the key fob will not release the pontoon gate solo before eight or after six, and the section voted this at the spring meeting, nineteen to four, so tonight is information, not debate. Krall: Then I am information: the fob system fails the early birds whose buddy cancels at dawn. Voss: A fair point inside an unfair habit. The answer is the whiteboard pairing list Mrs. Egan runs for the Tuesday group, extended to all mornings: post your slot the night before, the board pairs strangers, and strangers have become the section's best safety feature, because nobody skips a check on someone they just met. Egan: The Tuesday list paired 300 swims this season, no incidents, two marriages. Laughter. Voss: The safety record credits the first number; the section takes no position on the second. Remaining items: the rescue board needs a new fin, 60 dollars, approved by show of hands; the ice swim in January caps at twenty entrants with the doctor present as before; and the heron, members are reminded, has right of way at the reed end, by long custom and because he was here first. Closed 8:15.
question: How many solo swims does the sign-in board show for the season?

passage: Transcript, trustees meeting, the Harkness Organ Restoration Fund, decision session on the builder. Chair Fenchurch: Two tenders, both from firms we respect, and a decision tonight, as the church council meets Thursday. Summaries. Secretary Olamide: Tender one, Willard and Fisk: full restoration, 96,000 dollars, thirty months, organ out of the church for the middle year, everything to their workshop. Tender two, the Brandt workshop: 84,000, twenty months, all work done in situ with the organ playable, their phrase, for most of the period, using a method their letter describes at length and Mr. Petrie will now translate. Organist Petrie: Brandt restores rank by rank, one soundboard at a time, so the organ limps but plays: weddings, funerals, Sunday services continue with reduced stops. Willard takes it away and returns it perfect, but the church is silent, or rather electronic, for a year, and the last time this parish heard an electronic substitute, the letters ran in the newsletter for months. Fenchurch: Quality difference, honestly? Petrie: Honestly: Willard's workshop finish is the finest in the trade, and on the reed voicing in particular they have no equal. Brandt's work is excellent and their in situ method is proven at three churches I have visited and played. The difference is real and it is small, and it costs 12,000 dollars and a silent year. Trustee Mrs. Kohl: I sat with the funeral question all week. In twenty months, this parish will bury people. Whose mother is buried to a loudspeaker so the reeds can be voiced finer than anyone in this room can hear? Silence, noted. Fenchurch: Motion: the Brandt tender at 84,000, the 12,000 difference held as contingency, and Mr. Petrie to visit Brandt's current site monthly with report. Moved Kohl, seconded Olamide. Carried, five to nil. The chair will tell Willard and Fisk themselves, by visit, not letter; a firm of that standing is owed a chair in person.
question: How long is the Brandt workshop's restoration period?

passage: Minutes recorded verbatim, Pettifer Lane Toy Library, annual meeting, item four onward. Coordinator Nash: Item four, the inventory. The library holds 640 toys, of which 61 are presently in the repair basket, and the repair basket, let the minutes be honest, is a euphemism for Mr. Danby's garage. Danby: The garage returns 30 this month. The wooden garage itself, the toy one, wants hinges I am still sourcing. The ride-on tractor is beyond me: the axle casting snapped, and welding cast is a specialist job quoted at 90 dollars, against a new tractor at 110. Nash: And yet. Danby: And yet the tractor is the most borrowed toy in the library's history, 214 loans by the card, and the card is a social document: half this village learned to steer on it, and their children queue for it now. I move we weld. Mrs. Iqbal: Second, on one condition: the welder photographs the repair for the newsletter, because a village that mends things should show its children what mending looks like. Carried, everyone, one abstention from the treasurer on principle, the principle being arithmetic, she asks it recorded, not sentiment. Nash: So recorded, and the treasurer is thanked for losing gracefully, as is her custom. Item five: the toddler group asks for a second session on Thursdays; volunteers exist if the heating can be afforded, and the heating, the treasurer notes with visible pleasure, can, the coal club discount having come through at last. Approved. Item six: the summer toy amnesty returned 41 long-lost items, including the fire engine missing since 2019, found, the returning family confesses, inside the sofa they were discarding, and the fire engine is hereby retired to the display shelf with honors as the library's most patient toy. Meeting closed 8:50, biscuits acknowledged, Mrs. Ferris thanked, the urn, as ever, temperamental.
question: How many loans does the ride-on tractor's card show?

passage: Transcript, crew meeting, the ferry Maren Rose, winter schedule and the new deckhand, master presiding in the mess. Master Lindgren: Three things, then coffee properly. First, the winter timetable, posted this morning: five crossings weekdays, down from seven, first boat 6:40 as always, because the shift workers at the cannery built their lives on the 6:40 and the company agrees the 6:40 is not touched, whatever else winter does. Saturdays four crossings, Sundays two, and the Sunday evening boat is now the 17:15, not the 18:30, so tell your passengers, because for the first month it will be us standing on the pier explaining. Mate Okafor: The football crowd will miss the 18:30 home leg. Lindgren: The football crowd petitioned the office, and the office answered with the charter rate, and the football club, to everyone's astonishment, has chartered: the 19:45 on match Sundays, club pays, supporters ride free with a season ticket. The office is calling it community spirit; the manifest will call it the football boat. Second thing: ice protocol refresher is Thursday at the terminal, mandatory, including for me, and the instructor this year is Mrs. Halvorsen from the pilot service, who broke us all of three bad habits last year and has, she writes, found two more. Third: welcome Elsa Brandt, deckhand, starting Monday, who comes to us from three seasons on the fjord boats north, which means she knows more about ice than this entire mess deck and will be treated accordingly: as the resource, not as the new girl who makes coffee. The coffee rota, for the record, says the master makes it Mondays, and the master does. Questions? Okafor: Does the football boat need crew? Lindgren: Volunteers at time and a half, list on the door, and I am first on it. Meeting done; the kettle is mine.
question: At what time does the Sunday evening boat now run?

passage: Verbatim record, Silverbeck Arts Trust, commissioning panel, the riverside sculpture decision. Chair Adeyinka: Three shortlisted proposals, budget 40,000 dollars, site the old ferry steps. The panel has visited all three studios. Final statements from the file, then the vote. Secretary Voll: Proposal one, Kreuz: bronze ferryman, figurative, 38,000. Public comments from the exhibition: 214 cards, largely warm, the word proper appears 31 times, as in a proper statue. Proposal two, Mbeki-Larsen: steel and river stone, abstract, the form based on the wake pattern of the old ferry, 34,000; comment cards 190, split sharply, the word bold appearing 28 times, deployed by both camps with differing intent. Laughter, noted. Proposal three, the Harrow studio: a working tide bell of cast bronze, rung by the river itself at high water, 39,500, cards 260, and one comment the panel asked to have read into the record, from a child's handwriting: the river gets to talk. Adeyinka: Panel discussion is minuted in summary by agreement, save for Dr. Pell's point, which the panel asked recorded in full. Dr. Pell: Statues are of the past, and this river has plenty. The bell is of the present tense: it will ring at hours no one chooses, in the night, in the flood, when the last bus has gone, and the town will learn its river's moods by ear within a year. No plaque teaches that. We are not buying an object, we are buying a relationship. Adeyinka: The vote: Kreuz one, Mbeki-Larsen one, the tide bell five. The tide bell is commissioned at 39,500, with the child's comment card, if the family consents, cast into the bell's inscription band. The panel further asks that the Kreuz maquette be acquired for the library case at 800 dollars, funds from the education line, because a town that argues this well about art should keep the argument visible. Carried, seven to nil. Closed 9:20.
question: How much does the tide bell proposal cost?

passage: Transcript, quarterly meeting, Fenn Street Repair Cafe volunteers, the numbers and the lamp problem. Coordinator Brill: Quarter's numbers first, because they are cheerful: eleven sessions, 340 items brought in, 261 repaired on the spot, 40 sent home with parts ordered and instructions, 39 declared honorably dead, which is a 77 percent save rate on the spot and 88 counting the homework. Applause, noted, self-inflicted. The textile table remains the champion: Mrs. Osei's team repaired 84 garments and radicalized, her word, eleven new menders through the visible mending class. Brill: Now the lamp problem, and I need the room's decision. One third of everything through the door is lamps, and our electrical bench, which is Gerhard and, on alternate weeks, Priya, turns away lamp owners every session by four o'clock. Gerhard: I love lamps. I am one man. Every lamp is the same three faults and I could teach a patient twelve-year-old the testing sequence in an hour. Brill: Which is the proposal: a lamp school. One session a month becomes teaching only: bring your lamp, learn the sequence, test it yourself under supervision, leave with a working lamp and the knowledge. The insurance question I have already asked: covered, provided the tester Gerhard signs off each repair before it leaves, same as now. Priya: The queue objection: teaching halves the day's throughput. Gerhard: And doubles next year's benches. Every mender in this room was once a queue. Mrs. Osei: The textile table began as exactly this, six years ago, with four students and my mother's machine. The lamp school is how benches are born. I move it. Priya: Seconded, and I will co-teach; his sequence has one step in the wrong order. Gerhard: It does not. Priya: Bring your lamp Thursday. Laughter. Brill: Motion carried, all hands. First lamp school the second Saturday of next month, posters by Kim, who also asks it minuted that the accordion from session nine has been claimed at last, and the hall is once again silent, for which the hall committee is grateful. Closed 7:55.
question: How many items were repaired on the spot during the quarter?

passage: Minutes, verbatim, Dunsmore Astronomical Society, the dark sky campaign, strategy session. President Okonjo: The petrol station lighting. Update from the delegation. Vice President Sarti: We met the owner, Mr. Havel, on Tuesday, and I want the minutes to correct the society's assumptions, because we went in braced for a fight and were ambushed by reasonableness. He inherited the canopy lights with the franchise; the specification was written by the fuel company in 2009; and when Elena showed him the meter reading from the car park, 41 lux where the sky survey wants 2, his answer was, and I quote, I sell petrol, not glare, what do you want me to fit? Elena Voss: I sent him the shielded fixture specification Wednesday. His electrician quotes 2,400 dollars for the full canopy refit, and Mr. Havel's counterproposal is this: he pays half if the society funds half, and in exchange we name the station in the dark sky leaflet as a supporter, which, he was frank, is worth advertising to him, since the astronomy campers from the reserve buy his coffee at dawn. Okonjo: The society's lighting fund holds 1,900. Half is 1,200. Voss: And the county dark sky grant reimburses shielding conversions at up to 50 percent, applications monthly, our case is textbook. If the grant lands, our net cost is 600. Treasurer Bly: I confirm the fund can carry 1,200 pending the grant without touching the telescope line. Okonjo: Motion: fund 1,200, apply for the grant, leaflet acknowledgment, and Elena drafts a one page shielded lighting guide for the other four businesses on the ridge road, because the petrol station just became our showroom. Moved Sarti, seconded Bly. Carried, fourteen to nil. And the minutes will record Mr. Havel's sentence in full, because the campaign has searched two years for its slogan and a petrol station owner wrote it: glare serves nobody. Closed 9:05, skies clear, the car park, for now, still 41 lux, but not for long.
question: What did the meter read in the petrol station car park?

passage: Transcript, board meeting, Cobble Hythe Sea Shanty Festival, the licensing condition crisis, extraordinary session. Chair Pratt: You have all read the council's letter. The festival license this year carries a new condition: amplified music ends at 22:00, not 23:00, after last year's complaint. Singular. One complaint. Secretary Mbatha: One complaint, from one address, and I have, through entirely legal churchyard gossip, established the address: the holiday let on Anchor Lane, occupied that weekend by visitors who had, the booking site review confirms, come for a quiet coastal retreat and found, I am quoting the review, four hundred bearded men singing about drowning. Laughter, sustained. Chair Pratt: The review gave us two stars and the town five. Nonetheless, the condition stands unless appealed, and the appeal window closes Friday. Options. Treasurer Finch: Appeal costs 400 in fees and, per our solicitor, likely fails; councils rarely reverse a first-year condition, they prefer to review after the event. Or accept it, and here is my arithmetic: the final hour is the bar's best hour, worth roughly 3,000 across the weekend, but, and I checked with the chapel choir, the unamplified singing tradition, the midnight sing on the harbor steps, needs no license at all, being neither amplified nor, legally, a performance, but a gathering. Mbatha: The midnight sing is how the festival began in 1987, before we could afford a single speaker. Finch: Then the program simply says: amplified stages close at ten, and at half past ten, the harbor steps, bring a voice. We lose an hour of bar takings and regain the thing everyone over fifty says we lost. Pratt: The board will now be sentimental in the direction of profit, my favorite governance. Motion: accept the condition, no appeal, midnight sing restored as the closing event, and a courteous invitation sent to whoever books the Anchor Lane holiday let for festival weekend, with earplugs and two free tickets. Moved Finch, seconded Mbatha. Carried, six to nil. Closed 8:30.
question: At what time must amplified music now end under the new condition?

passage: Verbatim minutes, the Pightle Community Orchard trust, emergency meeting, the digger question. Chair Renata Voss: Monday morning, as everyone now knows, a contractor's digger arrived at the east boundary and began stripping the headland for the fiber cable, eleven meters inside our boundary, and was stopped, the minutes should record exactly, by Mrs. Cotterill, aged 81, who stood in front of it with her dog and her library book until the driver, in his own words, phoned the office for someone above my pay grade. Applause, noted. Mrs. Cotterill: The book was quite long. I was prepared. Voss: Damage assessment, from Aldo. Orchardist Aldo Kray: Sixty meters of headland scraped, the sloe hedge grubbed along that length, and the roots of two apple trees, the Kessler pippin and the old perry pear, run under that strip; both trees will live, but the scrape cut feeder roots, and I want compensation to include two years of monitoring, because damage to a tree tells its truth slowly. Voss: The company's position, received this morning by email: full apology, their subcontractor misread the wayleave plan, the correct route is the road verge, and they ask for our costs. They expect a number. Kray: Then the number: hedge replanting at proper density, 1,400. Headland reseeding, 300. Tree monitoring, two years, 600. And the intangible, which I refuse to price at zero: the hedge was 40 years old and hedges are time, so I propose they fund, additionally, the community fruit hedge along the north path we have postponed for five years, 2,100, as time owed. Total: 4,400, and we call it settled without lawyers, whose fees would exceed it by Thursday. Voss: Motion: Kray's figure, one letter, settlement within 30 days or the tone changes. Moved, seconded, carried eight to nil. Final entry: the trust records its thanks to Mrs. Cotterill, appoints her honorary warden of the east boundary, and notes her request that the title come with no duties whatsoever, which is granted, the trust holding that she has already performed them all. Closed 7:40.
question: How far inside the boundary did the digger begin stripping?
